source_tamil_lines: உன் முதுகை கொஞ்சம் திரும்பி பாரு பின்னாலே
ஊழல் ஊழல் என்று தினம் பாடினாயே பாட்டு
உன் முகத்தை நீயே ஒரு கண்ணாடியில் காட்டு
பெரும் தூண் என்று உன் தலையில் வீழுமப்பா
english_lines: Justice for the heart,
A sword for the shoulder,
A radiant gem, filled full —
Wear it. Like cotton,
Are all the many sufferings;
Before your gaze — a great fire,
Without deceit, without enmity, without gambling,
So that all the people of the world may live,
The justice poet Bharathi sang,
Justice for the heart joined with truth,
Before you speak of another person's fault,
Turn your own back a little and look behind,
The counsel of the noble,
Do not stop it merely at the lips,
Imprint it in your heart, anne,
The paths shown by the great ones of thought,
Heap them up as deeds, anne,
(One person)
Saying, 'Let us bring down caste and religions,'
Buddha and Gandhi gave their teaching,
To see God in the poor person's smile,
Arignar Anna was born here,
Let us do our duty; let us gain our rights,
Let us wipe away folly,
Let us live as human beings,
(One person)
'Corruption, corruption' — every day you sang that song,
Show your own face in a mirror yourself,
This work of casting empty blame is not for you,
It won't do, appa,
It will fall on your head like a great pillar, appa,
(One person).
notes: The opening `நெஞ்சுக்கு நீதியும் / தோளுக்கு வாளும்` remains the heart/justice and shoulder/sword pairing; the compact `சுடர்மணி பூண் / பஞ்சுக்கு நேர்` syntax is kept visibly segmented rather than rewritten into a smoother new stanza.
`அண்ணே` and `அப்பா` remain audible as `anne` and `appa`, retaining the direct-address register.
Bharathi, Buddha, Gandhi and Arignar Anna remain named exactly as the source's rhetorical chain names them.
`சாதி மதங்களை சாய்ப்போம்` remains the direct call to bring down caste and religions; the political-social force is not euphemized.
The repeated `(ஒருவர்)` cue is rendered literally as `(One person)` rather than silently expanded into the whole opening line.

translator_notes: This two-page song moves from ethical imagery to self-critique, anti-caste/religious reform, duty/rights and an accusation against corruption rhetoric; the English keeps those shifts explicit.
PDF provenance remains one continuous record across pages 86–87.
This is a literary source-faithful translation, not a singable adaptation.
